scenario: Embodied AI has 10 papers today, one with a deep dive. The deep-dive paper finds that the longer a flow-matching VLA (vision-language-action model) executes blind, the fewer numerical integration steps it should use when generating actions. On long-horizon simulation tasks π0 goes from 86.9% to 90.5% success while inference gets several times faster, and the effect holds on a real robot. Several others cover robot data: OXE-AugE extends the OXE dataset to more robot embodiments, NVIDIA open-sources a robot data labeling engine, and one paper uses reinforcement learning to generate more efficient and diverse demonstrations. Teams deploying VLAs can start with the first paper.

papers.title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
papers.authors: Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang, Ziheng He, Xiangnan Wu, Yingda Li, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
papers.abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $π_0$, $π_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon-Depth-VLA/
papers.scoring_note: Training-free joint horizon/solver tuning across three VLA backbones and real Franka.
papers.summary: In flow-matching vision-language-action models, solver steps and execution horizon turn out to be coupled, and the best setting can reverse. These models start from random noise and use a numerical solver to push it step by step into a smooth action chunk. Deployment usually tunes the two separately: the horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver steps stay high for accuracy. Under frequent replanning, fewer solver steps do hurt, but ==when a long stretch of actions runs open loop, fewer solver steps actually help==, because coarse integration keeps actions closer to the mean trajectory and limits compounding drift. Executing 5 actions at a time, 10 solver steps win. Executing 20 at a time, 2 solver steps win. The pattern holds across benchmarks and real robots, cutting latency and raising success without training.

papers.title: OXE-AugE: A Large-Scale Robot Augmentation of OXE for Scaling Cross-Embodiment Policy Learning
papers.authors: Guanhua Ji, Harsha Polavaram, Lawrence Yunliang Chen, Sandeep Bajamahal, Zehan Ma, Simeon Adebola, Chenfeng Xu, Ken Goldberg
papers.abstract: Large and diverse datasets are needed for training generalist robot policies that can control a variety of robot embodiments--robot arm and gripper combinations--across diverse tasks and environments. As re-collecting demonstrations and retraining for each new embodiment are prohibitively costly, we study whether existing robot data can be augmented to improve transfer and generalization across embodiments. The Open X-Embodiment (OXE) dataset, which aggregates demonstrations from over 60 robot datasets, has been widely used for training generalist policies. However, it is highly imbalanced: the top four robot types account for over 85% of its real data, which risks overfitting to robot--scene combinations. We present AugE-Toolkit, a scalable robot augmentation pipeline, and OXE-AugE, a high-quality open-source dataset that augments OXE with 9 different robot embodiments. OXE-AugE provides over 4.4 million trajectories, more than triple the size of the original OXE. We conduct a systematic study of how scaling robot augmentation impacts cross-embodiment learning. Results suggest that augmenting datasets with diverse arms and grippers improves policy performance not only on the augmented robots, but also on unseen robots and even the original robots under distribution shifts. In physical experiments, fine-tuning generalist policies such as OpenVLA and $\pi_0$ on OXE-AugE improves success rates by 24-45% on unseen robot-gripper combinations across four real-world manipulation tasks. Project website: https://OXE-AugE.github.io/.
papers.scoring_note: Open OXE augmentation toolkit and 4.4M trajectories; 24–45% physical success gains on four tasks across unseen embodiments.
papers.summary: Generalist robot policies must control many arm and gripper combinations, but recollecting data and retraining for each new robot is too costly. The widely used Open X-Embodiment dataset gathers over sixty robot datasets yet is badly imbalanced: the top four robot types make up over 85% of its real data. This paper builds an augmentation toolkit that extends existing demonstrations to nine other arm and gripper combinations, yielding OXE-AugE with 4.4 million trajectories, more than three times the original. The abstract gives the scale and findings but not how actions are converted to the new robots. Experiments show ==diverse robot augmentation helps not only the augmented robots== but also unseen robots and the original robots under distribution shift.

papers.title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines
papers.authors: Sicong Leng, Yunze Man, Zhiqi Li, Jing Wang, Yuhe Zhang, Ryan Punamiya, Siddharth Patki, Kaiyuan Zheng, Zi-ang Cao, Zhiding Yu, Sifei Liu, Danfei Xu, Ben Levin, Jan Kautz, Yuke Zhu, Johan Bjorck, Linxi "Jim" Fan
papers.abstract: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly 125 times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Florais battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.
papers.scoring_note: Open robotics data engine used for GR00T; 200000 hours/day on 512 GB300s; industrial-scale evidence.
papers.summary: Training robot foundation models takes huge amounts of labels: deployments need task-success judgments, reinforcement-learning post-training needs per-step process scores, and pretraining needs timestamped captions to filter data. NVIDIA has open-sourced Flora, the data engine used to train GR00T, where ==one model produces all three kinds of labels==. It sets the best scores on public captioning and reward benchmarks and matches GPT-6 Astra on internal tests. It is roughly 125 times cheaper and labels 200,000 hours of data a day on 512 GB300s.

papers.title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
papers.abstract: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo
papers.scoring_note: RL as demonstration generator; success 40→62% simulation, 39→78% real robot.
papers.summary: Imitation learning depends heavily on how widely its demonstrations cover the task, but collecting diverse successful demonstrations is expensive. This paper ==uses reinforcement learning as a data generator rather than a deployable controller==. DiscoDemo trains a generator where each latent code yields a different way to solve the task; training starts from states near the goal and gradually backs off. A diversity reward grows as the states visited under different latent codes lie farther apart in a learned representation, and it is given only to trajectories that complete the task. The generator's trajectories are filtered: failures are dropped, then any with unwanted robot-scene contact or excessive insertion force; the rest become a static dataset for a downstream visuomotor policy. Across four manipulation tasks, average downstream success versus the strongest baseline rises from 40% to 62% in simulation. On the real robot it rises from 39% to 78%.

papers.title: BitVLA: 1-bit Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotics Manipulation
papers.authors: Hongyu Wang, Chuyan Xiong, Ruiping Wang, Xilin CHEN
papers.abstract: Deploying powerful Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models on edge devices is limited by their massive size. In this paper, we take a deployment-oriented view of VLA training: we target efficiency through model design and optimization, rather than relying solely on post-hoc compression. Thus, we propose BitVLA, a fully native 1-bit VLA model for robotic manipulation, where every parameters is ternary, i.e., {-1,0,1}. BitVLA is built on the publicly available 1-bit LLM BitNet b1.58 2B4T, and is trained as a vision-language-action policy that inherits the compactness of 1-bit pretraining while retaining strong task performance. To further reduce the memory footprint of the vision backbone, we introduce Quantize-then-Distill, a post-training quantization-aware training strategy that compresses a full-precision vision encoder to 1.58-bit weights, while a full-precision teacher guides representation alignment during training. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, BitVLA matches the performance of the full-precision OpenVLA-OFT baseline, while reducing model memory by 11.0x and end-to-end latency by 4.4x. These results suggest a practical path toward training-time efficiency–accuracy co-design for embodied policies, enabling competitive manipulation capability on memory-constrained edge robotic platforms.
papers.scoring_note: Native ternary VLA and distilled low-bit vision; simulation plus physical evaluation.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models are too large for the edge devices robots carry. Rather than compressing after training, BitVLA uses extreme low-bit weights from the start: every parameter is one of minus one, zero or one, about 1.58 bits, conventionally called a 1-bit model, built on the open BitNet LLM. The vision encoder's weights are quantized to the same three values, and training pulls its image representations toward those of the original full-precision encoder. ==It matches the full-precision OpenVLA-OFT baseline== while cutting model memory by 11 times and end-to-end latency by 4.4 times.

papers.title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
papers.authors: Ayush Deshmukh, Nalin Agarwal, Elle Miller, Sethu Vijayakumar
papers.abstract: Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing $\textbf{225 consecutive $\mathbf{180^\circ}$ rotations (112.5 full rotations) at $\sim0.36 \;\text{rot/s}$}$ in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.
papers.scoring_note: Physical Shadow hand: 225 half-rotations; tactile ablation and concrete sim-to-real recipe.
papers.summary: People can spin Baoding balls in one palm without looking, but robots struggle to manipulate for long by touch alone. Blind policies can be trained in simulation, yet on a real dexterous hand contacts change constantly, tactile signals drift with motion, and simulated dynamics differ from reality. This paper uses only joint sensing and on-off tactile signals on a Shadow dexterous hand. In simulation it reproduces the real tactile sensor layout and the tendon-driven coupling of finger joints. It calibrates the on-off threshold of each tactile sensor separately, and adds two new randomizations: random limits on how fast actions can change, and randomly stuck tactile sensors. ==The policy transfers zero-shot to the real hand==, completing 225 consecutive half-turns in one continuous trial with no vision or object position.

papers.title: RealDexUMI: A Wearable Universal Manipulation Interface for Dexterous Robot Learning
papers.authors: Chaoyi Xu, Yixuan Jiang, Jiahui Huan, Yuhui Fu, Hao Yu Zhou, Weitian Yuan, Jiayi Yu, Wanpeng Zhang, Haoqi Yuan, Zongqing Lu
papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation requires demonstrations that preserve fine hand-object interactions while remaining executable at deployment. Existing pipelines either lose deployable dexterity through retargeting or embodiment conversion, or rely on robot-specific teleoperation that is costly to scale and often lacks intuitive, contact-aware control for dexterous data collection. We present RealDexUMI, a wearable universal manipulation interface built around a shared dexterous end-effector module that integrates a lightweight dexterous hand, in-hand vision, and fingertip tactile sensing. A palm-side isomorphic teleoperation glove maps human finger inputs to robot-hand joint commands, enabling real-time, retargeting-free, intuitive, and precise hand control. The shared hand and sensing modules yield zero-gap end-effector data, with matched in-hand observations, tactile signals, contacts, and hand actions between collection and deployment. Across eight real-robot tasks spanning fine-grained, contact-rich, long-horizon, and bimanual manipulation, policies trained on RealDexUMI data achieve an average success rate of 88.75%, generalize to unseen initial poses, and transfer across three embodiments.
papers.scoring_note: Matched wearable hand and tactile interface; eight real-robot tasks, retargeting-free demonstrations.
papers.summary: Dexterous hand demonstrations must keep fine hand-object contact while staying executable at deployment. Existing pipelines either lose fine motions when converting human hand movement to robot hand movement, or rely on costly, unintuitive robot-specific teleoperation rigs. RealDexUMI is a wearable collection device that uses the same dexterous hand module for collection and deployment, with in-hand cameras and fingertip touch sensors. A palm-side glove whose joints mirror the robot hand one to one, so bending a finger joint bends the matching robot joint with no motion conversion. ==Views, touch and actions match exactly between collection and deployment==. Across eight real-robot tasks, average success is 88.75%, and policies transfer across three robots.

papers.title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Bozhou Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
papers.abstract: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.
papers.scoring_note: Four real bimanual tasks; online supervised intervention updates within one hour; matched-baseline benefit limited.
papers.summary: When large robot foundation models are adapted to new tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations, the data rarely covers the hard states of deployment, such as contact, recovery from mistakes and precise alignment. TIDE puts robot execution, human takeover, learning and policy updates into one deployment session. The system records whether each action chunk came from the human or the policy, and training feeds that source label to the model as an extra input. When the robot runs on its own, the label is fixed to the human source, so the policy acts the way human takeovers did. ==No value function, reward model or action scorer is needed==, and updated policies go onto the robot at the end of each episode. On four real bimanual tasks, task progress and full completion beat both the starting policy and extra offline demonstrations, and the share of human takeovers falls.

papers.title: Regularised RL improves sim-to-real transfer
papers.authors: Danilo Vucetic, Mohamad H. Danesh, Florence Clerc, Hsiu-Chin Lin, Jonathan Tremblay
papers.abstract: Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) has provable robustness guarantees that should ease the transfer of policies from simulation to robots, known as sim-to-real. Yet, weakly regularised algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) remain the de facto choice in sim-to-real pipelines, while the practical benefits of regularisation for transfer remain poorly characterised. In this work, we study the sim-to-real performance of commonly used RL algorithms, with the aim of characterising the effects of regularisation on robotic performance. To that end, we derive Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a novel regularised RL algorithm based on the soft mellowmax value function, which carries strong robustness guarantees. On MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks, SMM-AC is competitive with baselines like Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). On real robots, SMM-AC achieves higher return, while exhibiting greater robustness to perturbations in observations, the environment, and dynamics than baselines. Together, these results demonstrate that regularised RL improves real-world policy deployment through better robustness to the sim-to-real gap, and changing real-world conditions.
papers.scoring_note: Regularised RL with robustness guarantees and physical-robot perturbation evaluation.
papers.summary: In theory, regularized reinforcement learning has provable robustness and should ease moving policies from simulation to real robots, yet pipelines still default to the weakly regularized PPO. This paper systematically compares common algorithms on sim-to-real transfer and derives a new one, SMM-AC. Instead of taking the maximum over action values when estimating the next state's value, it uses a smooth maximum: multiply the action values by a parameter ω, exponentiate, average, take the log and divide by ω. A large ω approaches the maximum and ω near 0 approaches the average; this kind of value function is proven robust to a wider set of perturbations. ==It matches the widely used RL algorithm SAC in MuJoCo simulation and earns higher returns on real robots==, staying steadier under perturbations to observations, environment and dynamics. The conclusion: regularization does narrow the sim-to-real gap.

papers.title: Revisiting Temporal Regularization for Smooth Control in Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: SungJae Ahn, Jeong Woon Lee, Kyoleen Kwak, Hyoseok Hwang
papers.abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning policies can produce nonsmooth action oscillations that hinder deployment on physical robots. Existing architectural and penalty-based approaches seek spatial smoothness by directly reducing sensitivity to changes in state inputs, but their broad constraints can degrade task performance as stronger smoothing is pursued. Temporal regularization instead constrains action differences along observed transitions, but has been considered unable to provide the spatial smoothness needed under observation noise. We revisit this assumption by proving that the temporal penalty bounds the expected action differences between current states sharing a next state, revealing a spatial effect that empirically extends to spatial smoothness. Building on this finding, we propose Conditioning for Action using only Temporal Smoothness (CATS), which combines a temporal penalty with linear ramp-up. We highlight temporal regularization's ability to provide spatial smoothness while better preserving task performance than explicit spatial regularization. Through linear ramp-up, CATS allows the policy to learn rewarding behavior before progressively smoothing its actions, improving return preservation and both temporal and spatial smoothness. Experiments in both simulation and the real world show that CATS substantially reduces action oscillation without degrading task performance, with little computational overhead.
papers.scoring_note: Temporal smoothness theory and low-overhead CATS recipe; simulation and real-world evaluation.
papers.summary: Robot policies trained with reinforcement learning often jitter between actions, which wears out motors on real hardware. Existing methods directly limit how much actions change when the input state changes slightly, but these broad constraints hurt task performance as smoothing grows. Penalizing only the difference between consecutive actions was thought unable to handle observation noise. This paper proves that when several current states lead to the same next state, the consecutive-step penalty also shrinks the action differences between them. That amounts to smoothing across nearby states, and experiments show the policy becomes steadier under observation noise. ==CATS uses only the consecutive-step penalty and ramps its weight up linearly from zero==, letting the policy learn to earn reward before it gradually smooths. In simulation and on real robots, action oscillation drops sharply with little loss in task performance.
